canberra.title: Elite road cycling’s ‘Milk Race’ returns as CDC Tour of Canberra
canberra.snippet: Australia’s elite road cycling league is locked in to return to Canberra for at least the next three years, and whoever wins stands...
canberra.content:
CDC founder and CEO Greg Boorer with Canberra road race cyclists Hayden Stevens and Lauren Bates at the launch of PSL’s CDC Tour of Canberra. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Australia’s elite road cycling league is locked in to return to Canberra for at least the next three years, and whoever wins stands a strong chance of becoming an Olympian.

It will literally be pedal to the metal for the Hertz ProVelo Super League’s (PSL) return from 26 to 28 February 2027, with the event to be known as the CDC Tour of Canberra.

CDC Data Centres founder and CEO Greg Boorer was once a competitive cyclist himself, and he used to come to Canberra every year as a teen to ride what was then known as the Milk Race (as it was sponsored by Canberra Milk).

“When the opportunity came along to breathe some life back into an absolutely iconic race, I didn’t need too much convincing,” he said.

“The opportunity to do something for the community here, and in a place that absolutely loves cycling … and to actually have kids being able to see the best cyclists in Australia, and increasingly from around the world, in their backyard [is incredible].

“This is a very, very small way of giving back to cycling, but also hopefully inspiring the next generation of Michael Rogers and Michael Matthews and Stephen Hodge to come out of Canberra.”

The CDC Tour of Canberra features a four-stage program over three days: an individual time trial at Black Mountain, a twilight street criterium in Canberra City, a circuit road race around the National Triangle, and a queen-stage road race at Stromlo Forest Park.

Former Olympic road cyclist Stephen Hodge first got noticed when he completed the original Canberra tours, and the last race led to his selection for the 1996 Atlanta Games.

“If you can make it in the Tour of Canberra, you’ve got real potential, and that’s what people overseas notice,” he said.

“Anyone who’s winning the Canberra Tour … next year could well be in the Olympics.”

Hertz ProVelo Super League co-founder Matt Wilson is involved in designing the course for the 2032 Brisbane Olympics road races (to be held on the Sunshine Coast).

He said bringing the event to Canberra was front of mind when he and Aaron Flanagan started the ProVelo Super League in 2025.

“I come from a professional cycling background so I, like every other young Australian cyclist, rode the Tour of Canberra and there’s just something hard about racing on these roads … the cream always came to the top,” Mr Wilson said.

“It’s just such a beautiful area to ride, and it’s just got such a strong club foundation.”

The final courses haven’t been finalised as there’s still some red tape and logistics to be sorted out, but they won’t be the same routes as during the Milk Race between 1989 and 1997.

But Mr Flanagan said the CDC Tour of Canberra would “set the bar” for the PSL’s other rounds on the calendar.

“We want to bring road cycling back to the communities – we’re about building a sports entertainment product, big screens, DJs, exciting racing,” he said.

“From the moment we launched the ProVelo Super League, there’s been this consistent and growing appetite to see elite road cycling return to Canberra.”

Hands Across Canberra CEO Genevieve Jacobs (centre) with Hertz ProVelo Super League founders Matt Wilson and Aaron Flanagan. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Other items on the tour agenda include community bike rides and possibly incorporating Canberra’s Enlighten Festival into the program.

The tour will be broadcast live on SBS for 2027 and is expected to go global from 2028.

Mr Flanagan said he was also excited to showcase Canberra to the world.

“People watch the Tour de France just because they can enjoy the scenery,” he said.

“That’s what we intend on doing with the Tour of Canberra … the way we’re going to be able to showcase this city to Australia and to the rest of the world is going to be amazing.”

In a stroke of fortuitous timing, the Tour of Canberra aligns with Hands Across Canberra’s big yearly fundraiser, the Canberra Day Appeal.

Hands Across Canberra is the event’s official charity partner for three years.

CEO Genevieve Jacobs said the timing couldn’t have been better.

“One of the things that we want to do with the Canberra Day Appeal is reach a really broad audience of people … [as we all] set the course for how we want to live this next year in Canberra together,” she said.

“The partnership is a great opportunity to bring together the community, sport and business, while celebrating a wonderful Canberra pastime and doing good things together.”

Plus, it’s a chance for the next generation of Canberra cyclists to make their mark.

With the 2032 Brisbane Olympics just around the corner, it may be a chance to see history in the making.

Find out more about the upcoming CDC Tour of Canberra.

canberra.title: ACT unions combine for strike action to keep pay rise pressure on the government
canberra.snippet: An estimated 1000 union members have descended on the Legislative Assembly as part of strike action over pay negotiations. Members across...
canberra.content:
Hospice staff took their complaints to the Legislative Assembly. Photo: John Lomnicki.

An estimated 1000 union members have descended on the Legislative Assembly as part of strike action over pay negotiations.

Members across the Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) and Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) unions walked off the job on Thursday (29 October) morning for a two-hour strike, marching at Legislative Plaza before hopping on buses and heading back to work.

It follows 12 months of bargaining between unions and the ACT Government, with the government offering a 3 per cent pay rise each year for three years, plus built-in rises if wages don’t keep pace with inflation, which unions rejected as failing to meet cost-of-living pressures.

Unions involved in the strike are negotiating 17 individual Enterprise Bargaining Agreements, but are seeking across-the-board pay rises that don’t fall below CPI.

CFMEU ACT assistant branch secretary Michael Hiscox says any offer needs to keep pace with inflation.

“We’re here because the offer of the ACT Government is not enough to keep up with the cost of living,” he said.

“Our members are struggling to pay their bills; they’re struggling to live in Canberra with how expensive it is.

“Some of these workers here would be some of the lowest paid workers within the ACT Government, but they do some of the most critical work we need to keep the city running … Our view is that if these are the people that maintain our city, they deserve to live in it as well.”

Strike attendee and public health worker Darren Brown says negotiations had gone on long enough.

“We’re here today for the general strike because the government has not moved on their pay offer, which was overwhelmingly rejected by ACT public health workers,” he explained.

“We’ve been negotiating with the government for over 12 months now. They’re stalling, they have no solutions, they keep saying ‘we’re broke’.

“For a government to say ‘we’re broke’ is concerning.”

Representatives from multiple unions took part in the strike action on 29 October. Photos: John Lomnicki.

Mr Brown said that in his work as a union organiser, he frequently interacts with workers impacted by the Canberra health system’s current working conditions.

“We represent some of the lowest paid workers in health – food services people, hospital assistants, wards people – they’re at the lower end of the pay, and they’re significantly struggling, and the government has not recognised this in an appropriate way,” he says.

“Workers come on a daily basis when I visit the Canberra Hospital and say ‘we’re struggling on this pay. We cannot put food on the table.’”

For CPSU ACT Regional Secretary Maddy Northam, the strike’s scale was a big step forward, as industrial action was first flagged seven months ago.

“This was the first time since self-government [in the ACT] that we have seen strike action of this magnitude across so many directorates, so many enterprise agreements, and so many unions,” she says.

“They are sending a clear message to Andrew Barr: enough is enough, put a clear offer on the table.

“Until the government comes to the table with a fair offer that keeps pace with the cost of living, workers will keep voting no.

“They [workers] are prepared to fight; they are prepared to stand in solidarity with each other for a fair pay rise.”

The Australian Education Union (AEU) ACT Branch announced it has suspended next week’s planned two-hour rolling stoppages, with a new pay and conditions offer to be provided by 9 November.

ACT branch president Angela Burroughs says the news was a welcome development following more than a year of bargaining and months of industrial action.

“Our members would much rather be in their classrooms supporting students than taking industrial action,” she says.

“With a new offer now promised, we believe the reasonable thing to do is give the government the opportunity to deliver it.

“Our expectation is that the revised offer will address members’ concerns about staffing, class sizes, safety and pay.”

But the looming cloud of 2027 school budgets, and the confusion that remains around the process, means the government’s commitment to public education will be judged on more than the outcome of enterprise bargaining.

“Regardless of what the revised offer contains, the government still has serious questions to answer about its proposed cuts to school budgets for 2027,” Ms Burroughs says.

“Schools are facing significant budget reductions, with some already making difficult decisions about staffing, programs and student support. A new enterprise agreement does not resolve those concerns.

“You cannot expect schools to deliver better outcomes for students while asking them to do more with less. The government must ensure every public school has the budget it needs to properly staff its classrooms and support its students.”

canberra.title: Stranger allegedly targets multiple women outside fitness studio
canberra.snippet: Multiple women were walking to or from a fitness studio in central Canberra when they were allegedly harassed or threatened by the same m...
canberra.content:
29 October 2026

Christopher Joseph Lichtwark allegedly threatened women over multiple days earlier this month. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Multiple women were walking to or from a fitness studio in central Canberra when they were allegedly harassed or threatened by the same man over two days.

ACT Policing began a public manhunt to find the man responsible for the alleged behaviour before arresting 42-year-old Christopher Joseph Lichtwark of Dickson.

The ACT Magistrates Court heard it alleged he first tried to kick a woman when she was walking outside the Braddon fitness studio at around 5 am on 15 October 2026.

Police released this image while trying to identify 42-year-old Christopher Joseph Lichtwark. Photo: ACT Policing.

Shortly afterwards, another distressed woman went into the studio claiming she had been harassed outside. She alleged she’d seen Lichtwark approach three other women on the street, before they screamed and moved away.

The court heard how around 5 am on 16 October, another woman alleged he approached her near the studio and asked her about the cost of a membership.

“Tell me how much it costs or I’ll f-k you up, c-t,” he allegedly said before throwing a bottle at her.

Lichtwark, sitting in the Magistrates Court on Thursday (29 October), laughed when he heard this allegation.

“Completely made up, your honour,” he said.

The court also heard it alleged he ran at another woman on the street near the studio later that same morning.

“There’s a degree of persistence over two days,” Special Magistrate Michael Cowen said of the allegations.

“Targeting females particularly is very serious, concerning behaviour.”

Lichtwark was charged with two counts each of assault and affray before he applied for bail, which the prosecutor opposed.

“The nature of the offending is quite bizarre, and it appears that the defendant is fixated, for whatever reason, on this address,” the prosecutor claimed.

“They were strangers to the defendant … all complainants have expressed concerns for their safety.

“They are now anxious to go to that particular business.”

Lichtwark’s lawyer from Legal Aid argued supervision by authorities would go a long way to ameliorating the risks of his release and would help him manage his mental health conditions.

The lawyer suggested his charges may even be dealt with on mental health grounds.

She said Lichtwark told her he was on Centrelink’s JobSeeker payments, wanted to return to work in the landscaping and labouring industry, and was “terrified” of going into custody for the first time if bail was refused.

But Special Magistrate Cowen said he was concerned Lichtwark may endanger the safety of women if he was released and refused bail.

“Ah yeah, thanks your honour,” Lichtwark said before he was led out of the courtroom.

The matter was adjourned to 25 November. No pleas were entered.

canberra.title: Where’s the payout? ACT orders review into clubs’ Community Contributions Scheme
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has agreed to review how it distributes millions of dollars in poker machine revenue to community organisations after ...
canberra.content:
ACT Government has agreed to review how it calculates and distributes poker machine contributions. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The ACT Government has agreed to review how it distributes millions of dollars in poker machine revenue to community organisations after an audit found all 19 club licences examined failed to fully comply with reporting requirements.

The review, secured through a motion by Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti in the Legislative Assembly, will examine the transparency of the Community Contributions Scheme, the value of non-cash donations and whether community groups are receiving genuine benefits.

It will also consider the feasibility of a centralised, independent fund to distribute contributions, as the government moves ahead with gambling reforms expected to reduce poker machine revenue.

Under ACT law, clubs operating poker machines must contribute at least 8 per cent of their net gaming machine revenue to community purposes. Last year, Canberra clubs reported nearly $7 million in community contributions, but Ms Vassarotti questioned how much represented direct financial support.

She said information obtained from the government showed all 19 club licences examined in a 2024–25 audit had breached reporting obligations.

“For years, there hasn’t been a single detailed audit to check if these venues are meeting their basic obligations. Now, the single audit that was conducted proves exactly why we need proper and routine regulation,” she said.

Ms Vassarotti also questioned whether clubs should be allowed to count in-kind contributions, such as providing rooms and facilities, towards their mandatory obligations.

“If clubs are serious about earning a social license, they can’t keep using empty rooms as multi-hundred-dollar tax write-offs,” she said.

The review follows earlier concerns about the scheme.

A 2018 Auditor-General’s report identified weaknesses in oversight, reporting and guidance, prompting reforms in 2019.

Gaming Reform Minister Marisa Paterson acknowledged the latest compliance problems but said they primarily involved reporting and administrative processes.

“Issues identified related primarily to reporting practices and administrative processes rather than the objectives of the scheme itself,” she told the Assembly.

Dr Paterson supported the review, saying community contributions needed to deliver genuine benefits. She said the government was already working with clubs on diversification following an independent inquiry into the industry’s future. A joint clubs transition governance group and a dedicated concierge service would help clubs explore alternative revenue streams and development opportunities.

However, the Canberra Liberals warned that the government’s gambling reforms could undermine the funding community organisations currently receive.

Opposition Leader Mark Parton argued that replacement funding must be secured before measures reducing club revenue take effect.

“Changing who distributes the money doesn’t replace revenue that’s disappeared,” he said.

He questioned whether the government had adequately assessed the combined financial impact of its reforms on clubs, community organisations and Territory revenue.

The government’s proposals include mandatory account-based gambling, restrictions on cash withdrawals at venues and reducing poker machine authorisations to no more than 1000 by 2045. Mr Parton said community clubs such as Vikings supported numerous grassroots sporting organisations and warned that centralising contributions could weaken established funding relationships.

ClubsACT chief executive officer Craig Shannon echoed those concerns, calling for the reforms to be withdrawn and reworked until financial safeguards were established.

“The motion seeks a report by the final sitting week of 2027. Sporting organisations and charities need certainty before their support is affected,” he said.

“A review after funding has disappeared will not pay their bills or restore a cancelled program.”

Mr Shannon also questioned the absence of a costed transition package and the innovation fund previously promised to help clubs diversify.

Dr Paterson said any future funding model must consider charities, cultural organisations and other community groups, not just sport. The review will now examine whether the existing scheme can provide transparent, sustainable community funding as the Territory reduces its reliance on poker machines.

australia.title: Study of 100,000 Australians seeks causes of mental health disorders and early onset cancer
australia.snippet: Sax Institute is recruiting for 18 and Up, an intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing which follows its landmark 45 and Up study ...
australia.content:
Researchers hope to better understand the drivers of major health challenges facing younger people, such as mental illness and rising cancer rates, through the recruitment of 100,000 people for Australia’s largest intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing.

The independent and not-for-profit research institute the Sax Institute, on Thursday launched the 18 and Up study, which will follow the health of those aged 18 to 45 throughout their lives.

Two decades ago, the institute started 45 and Up, now the largest population-based cohort study in the southern hemisphere, with more than 267,000 participants ranging in age from 45 to older than 100.

Since then, participants have been repeatedly surveyed and their responses linked to other datasets, leading to significant discoveries about smoking, dementia prevention, and differences in cardiovascular outcomes between men and women.

18 and Up’s scientific director, Adjunct Prof Justine Gatt, said there was a lack of long-term data for younger generations, with existing studies often only giving researchers information from a snapshot in time.

“Almost two in five young Australians aged 16 to 24 experienced a mental disorder in the past year, and that number has been rising,” Gatt, a neuroscientist and mental health researcher said. “Yet we still lack the long-term evidence needed to understand why.”

Suicide is the leading cause of death among Australians aged 15 to 44, and researchers have said there is an urgent need to understand and address driving factors to improve prevention efforts and mental health treatments.

Children and grandchildren of 45 and Up participants will be invited to participate, which Gatt said will help researchers understand how health is influenced by a complex mix of family history, lived experiences and social conditions, and how these factors interact across generations.

The CEO of the Sax Institute, Dr Martin McNamara, said along with mental health, questions around cancer will also be an important part of the initial round of surveys.

Since 2000, there has been an increase in early-onset cancers – defined as those diagnosed beyond adolescence but before the age of 50 – in Australia and other parts of the world. This includes bowel, thyroid, breast and other cancers.

While scientists think increased screening, changing lifestyles and different exposures to risk factors in early life and young adulthood may all be factors, there have been calls for urgent research to better understand these and other influences.

Participants will be asked about health, lifestyle, social circumstances and background and, with consent, this information will be linked to other health records, such as cancer registries and Medicare.

“It’s important we follow people over time … so that we can figure out ways to fix and re-organise our health and care systems,” McNamara said.

“We’ll have a really good picture of their lives, the things that are important to them, their education, their employment, where they live.”

The study will evolve with participants to receive age-relevant questions, and emerging health conditions or pandemics will be factored in. It is being funded by a $4.5m National Health and Medical Research Council grant, with recruitment beginning in November.

Professor of epidemiology and public health at the Australia National University, Emily Banks, is a former scientific director at the Sax Institute who used 45 and Up study data to reveal in 2025 that smoking-related illnesses kill 66 Australians every day – more than previously thought.

Banks said large-scale cohort studies are powerful as they give researchers a window into the population and help detail what people are exposed to during their lives. She said the 45 and Up data has become an important collaborative resource.

It has been used by more than 800 researchers worldwide.

“We’ve had hundreds of researchers using the data. We also have around 10% of the population of New South Wales in that age [45+] group in the study,” she said.

“Some of the biggest advances in health have come from using this kind of information.”

australia.title: Erin Patterson prepares for mushroom murders appeal ruling to learn if she could face retrial or longer jail term
australia.snippet: Victorian court to hand down decision on Friday on two appeals regarding Patterson’s triple murder case Get our breaking news email , fre...
australia.content:
Erin Patterson is set to find out if she could face a longer prison sentence or a new trial, as Victoria’s highest court hands down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.

The court of appeal is set to rule on the two appeals from 10am on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.

Patterson, 52, is not expected to attend the appeal decision in person.

She was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.

Patterson was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.

She has appealed against her convictions, while the director of public prosecutions appealed against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that it was manifestly inadequate.

In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.

Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.

Richard Edney, for Patterson, said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.

“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.

They also argued that the trial judge Christopher Beale erred in ruling that photos and videos related to mushrooms and found on an SD card in Patterson’s home was inadmissible, as it tended to support her evidence that she foraged for mushrooms.

During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.

When asked whether a longer non-parole period would essentially damn Patterson to dying behind bars, and had “some artifice of it being life with life”, Kissane told the court: “It has its harsh aspect to it, of course, we accept that.”

“But in our submission that is not a matter that is outweighed by the seriousness of the offending.”

There are several possible outcomes to Patterson’s appeal: leave to appeal is not granted; leave to appeal is granted, but her appeal dismissed; leave to appeal is granted, her appeal upheld and a retrial ordered; or her leave to appeal is granted, the appeal upheld, and acquittal entered.

If either of the final two decisions are handed down, there will be no need to rule on the DPP’s sentence appeal.

If not, either the appeal fails, or it succeeds and Patterson is resentenced by the court of appeal.

australia.title: Lawyers for Marist Brothers face questions over advice to keep serial offender out of ‘legal arena’
australia.snippet: A once-confidential letter says child sexual abuser might implicate senior church officials if allowed near ‘the legal arena’ upon his re...
australia.content:
Lawyers from a leading law firm for the Marist Brothers have been subpoenaed to explain a once-confidential document showing they advised the Catholic order to keep a serial offender out of “the legal arena”, suggesting he was too honest and might implicate senior church officials.

The offender was “regrettably up front” about his interactions with senior leadership, and could not be trusted to heed “suggestions” about “not dumping on others excessively”, the document says.

The Marist Brothers, a Catholic order, holds a shocking clergy abuse record and was found by the royal commission to have shuffled religious brothers across its network of Australian schools when complaints arose, allowing them continued access to children.

The order continues to face a string of civil claims from survivors, and is represented by major law firm Carroll & O’Dea, which has represented Catholic orders like the Marist and Christian Brothers for decades.

Now, one survivor has turned their scrutiny on to the conduct of Carroll & O’Dea itself, asking the ACT supreme court to issue subpoenas to individual lawyers to explain an explosive document in which the firm advised the head of the Marist order that a known offender should be kept away from legal processes because he has “high honesty and integrity levels” and might implicate senior church officials.

The case involves a survivor known as CQ who alleges he was abused by Brother Kostka Chute, or John William Chute, in 1985 and 1986 at Marist College Canberra. Chute is a serial offender who has attracted abuse complaints across Marist schools in Randwick, Bondi, Hunters Hill, Lismore, Coogee and Canberra.

CQ is alleging the Marist Brothers knew of abuse complaints against Chute but concealed them, something the order denies.

CQ’s lawyers this week resurfaced a once-confidential letter from Carroll & O’Dea to the then head of the Marist Brothers, Br Jeffrey Crowe, in 2009, penned after the lawyers visited Chute in Canberra’s jail.

The lawyers had gone to see Chute to better understand whether the Marist Brothers would be on the hook for civil claims relating to his abuse or whether it would be indemnified by the Catholic church’s insurance arm, a question that partly depended on whether it had prior knowledge of Chute’s offending.

The letter from Carroll & O’Dea advised Crowe that Chute was in “good form” but that he was: “Regrettably quite up front about various discussions with Provincials over the years including Br Charles, Br Quentin, Br Weldon. I think we will have some problems with indemnity in due course but not immediately.”

“Trouble is fundamentally he has high honesty and integrity levels and all of my ‘suggestions’ about not dumping on others excessively go out the window pretty quickly once there is a conversation under way.”

The lawyers advised the Marists that Chute – at that stage in jail for abusing six children – was not a “classic predator” and was a “good man with a fair bit of self-discernment”.

“We would need to keep him well away from the legal arena upon release,” the lawyers advised.

The airing of the contents of that letter caused significant issues in CQ’s case this week.

Porters Lawyers, the firm representing CQ, have subpoenaed two lawyers from Carroll & O’Dea to give evidence, and the court heard the move may raise potential issues alleging professional misconduct.

That required Carroll & O’Dea lawyers to themselves have legal representation and made its ongoing representation of the Marist Brothers impossible, because it would create a conflict of interest.

On Wednesday, Carroll & O’Dea told the court it would have to cease representing the Marist Brothers, causing a sudden halt to the trial and delays that will potentially stretch into next year.

The court also heard another matter against the Marist Brothers, also involving allegations against Chute, might be delayed.

Guardian Australia understands there are currently 15 cases against the Marist Brothers, represented by Carroll & O’Dea, involving Chute.

In a statement, the Marist Brothers said it could not comment because the proceedings were ongoing. A spokesperson said it expects the trial will resume “either later this year or in early 2027”.

Senior Marist Brothers have previously said that letter was sent as part of a chain of correspondence and was penned in the context of “serious doubts” about what Chute was claiming. The letter was examined in 2014 by the child abuse royal commission, which decided not to call its author to give evidence.

Crowe was asked about the letter at the royal commission, including whether it showed Chute was “seen as a liability that may impact upon the Marist Brothers and one that they need to sweep under the carpet”.

“I agree that he does give the impression there of some liability,” Crowe said. “However, I would also believe – because this, once again, is all part of another series of communications – that there were serious doubts as to the evidence being given by John Chute.”

Carroll & O’Dea was approached for comment.

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

world.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
world.snippet: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river wh...
world.content:
The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.

“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.

The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.

Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.

“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”

Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”

Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.

“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.

Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.

Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.

The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.

“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.

Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.

Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.

“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”

Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.

Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.

Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.

David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”

The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”

Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.

Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.

Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”

In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.

El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.

Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.

For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.

“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

world.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
world.snippet: Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces hav...
world.content:
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.

All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.

Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.

“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.

Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.

Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.

In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.

Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.

The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.

“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.

Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.

To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.

Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.
